title: Three Types of Motivation
author: fivetwelvethirteen
summary: The author presents a framework for classroom motivation organized by time scale: short-term motivators (choice, relevance, enjoyment, extrinsic rewards) that work quickly but burn out and involve tradeoffs; medium-term motivators (habits, success, accountability) that take longer to build but compound over weeks; and long-term motivators (community, identity, belonging) that are the most powerful but slowest and hardest to construct. Effective teaching uses all three together.
points: Motivation is defined as whether students actually attempt, put effort into, and persevere on tasks -- not a single fixable trait.
Short-term motivators (choice, relevance, enjoyment, extrinsic incentives) work immediately but must be constantly renewed and involve tradeoffs, e.g., equal learning across choices.
Medium-term motivators (habits, success, accountability) take longer to build but compound in power over days and weeks, and work best when established from the start of the year.
Long-term motivators (community, identity, belonging) are described as the most powerful but slowest to build, and are illustrated with a 'Mr. A vs. Mr. B' classroom story.
School culture can give some teachers a head start on building community while others must build it alone, making these motivators harder to transfer between contexts.
The author cautions against over-relying on community-building alone without other motivation strategies as backup.
The piece concludes that every teacher needs multiple motivation strategies across all three time scales that build on each other.
quotes: To me, the fundamental difference between motivation strategies is the time scale. Some motivation strategies are useful in the short term.

The first problem with short-term motivators is that they are short-term. These might work well in motivating students today or tomorrow, but to motivate them next week you’ll probably need to continue designing in opportunities for choice, or relevance, or enjoyment, or extrinsic incentives.
Medium-term motivators include habits, success, and accountability. These honestly sound totally boring.
The disadvantage of these strategies is that they don’t work right away, and they also require regular effort. Habits don’t happen overnight.

In this story, Mr. B is an expert at building community. That’s great! It’s an incredibly powerful tool for a teacher. But it’s also a tool that is often invisible to others, impossible to imitate, and slow to develop.
I do think that stepping back to consider whether a motivation strategy is short-term, medium-term, or long-term is a useful exercise.
Every teacher needs multiple motivation strategies, and every teacher should understand how those strategies fit together and build on each other.
